title: TSP with Predictions: Heatmap to Tour with Provable Guarantees
claim: With a perfect prediction, the algorithm's spanning path plus one closing edge already forms the optimal tour, needing no shortcutting.
layout: single panel, left-to-right, vertices on a line with one arc beneath
description: A single minimal black-and-white diagram of a TSP instance with points on a line. Nine filled black dots sit evenly spaced on a horizontal line and are joined by straight segments. The leftmost vertex is labeled 1 and the next two are labeled 2 and 3, followed by an ellipsis. The rightmost vertex is labeled n. A long curved arc runs below the line from vertex n back to vertex 1 and is labeled e. Together the line and the arc form the closed optimal tour. There is no color, no arrows and no legend. The eye goes first to the long closing edge e and the numbered endpoints. The picture is a toy example showing that the path T plus the edge e equals the optimal tour.
caption: Example instance of a TSP where the vertices are points on a line. Only the edges of the optimal tour $X^*$ are drawn. In the case with perfect prediction, i.e., $P=X^*$, Algorithm [ref] may choose the path from $1$ to $n$ as $T$ (there are multiple possibilities), $S = \{1, n\}$ and $J=\{e\}$ contains the edge $e$ connecting $n$ and $1$. Then $T+J = X^*$ and no short-cutting is needed.
abstract: The Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP) has long served as a benchmark for evaluating the strength of optimization techniques in the classical theory of algorithms. In recent efforts to apply ML to algorithmic problems, TSP has also become a natural testbed for the development of ML-based techniques. A common approach is to train a neural network to output a heatmap estimating the likelihood of each edge to be part of the optimal tour; however, converting such a heatmap into an actual tour remains a non-trivial and often computationally intensive step. In this work, we propose algorithms for transforming heatmaps into tours with theoretical guarantees linking the achieved approximation ratio to the quality of the provided heatmap. In the spirit of algorithms with predictions, our results can be described as $(1+2\fracÎ·{\mathrm{OPT}})$-approximation algorithms, where $Î·$ denotes the L1 distance between the prediction (heatmap) and an optimal solution (tour). Since the previous works lack such explicit guarantees, we compare our approach against them experimentally.
